speaker: Doctor
text:
Welcome to the clinic. I see you are a newborn presenting with respiratory distress; to help me understand your condition, please tell me your exact gestational age at birth.

Additionally, how would you describe the nature of your breathing difficulty—does it involve rapid breathing, grunting, or noticeable retractions?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, born at 33 weeks of gestation. The newborn is presenting with respiratory distress 2 hours after birth. The mother had an uneventful pregnancy until premature onset of labor. There was no significant prenatal care history mentioned.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you. Given your history of premature birth at 33 weeks and immediate respiratory distress, are there any signs of nasal flaring, grunting, or chest retractions you are noticing?

REQUEST TEST: Arterial_Blood_Gas
REQUEST IMAGES: Chest_X-Ray

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Blood_Gases: pH 7.30 (slightly acidic), PaCO2 50 mmHg (elevated), PaO2 60 mmHg (reduced), HCO3- 24 mEq/L; Chest_Radiograph: Fine reticular granulation with ground glass appearance on both lungs

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the data; the blood gas indicates respiratory acidosis with hypoxia, and the chest X-ray showing a "ground glass" appearance is highly characteristic of respiratory distress syndrome.

At 33 weeks gestation, this strongly suggests surfactant deficiency, but I must confirm if the baby required immediate resuscitation or shows signs of transient tachypnea of the newborn.

Was the infant intubated and placed on CPAP or mechanical ventilation immediately after birth?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Respiratory distress. I also have Grunting, Intercoastal and subcostal retractions, Peripheral cyanosis.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome (NRDS). The combination of prematurity (33 weeks), respiratory acidosis, hypoxia, and a chest X-ray showing "ground glass" appearance confirms surfactant deficiency.
